sections.h2: Virginia tax on a home sale profit
sections.html:
Capital gains get no special treatment in Virginia. Whatever you clear on the house is added to your Virginia return and run through the normal brackets.

Code of Virginia 58.1-320 sets those rates: 2% up to $3,000, 3% from $3,000 to $5,000, 5% from $5,000 to $17,000, and 5.75% above $17,000. Virginia's return opens with federal adjusted gross income, which means the federal main-home break flows through.

That makes the federal answer the one to get first. Whatever your federal return excludes carries over as the starting point on the Virginia return.

Tax or exclusionRate or limit
Virginia rate, first $3,0002%
Virginia rate, $3,000 to $5,0003%
Virginia rate, $5,000 to $17,0005%
Virginia rate above $17,0005.75%
Federal home sale exclusion$250,000 for one filer, $500,000 for a joint return

Qualifying takes 24 months of ownership and 24 months of living there as your primary home, both measured inside the five years that end on the closing date. Those months can come from different periods and don't need to be consecutive.

On a joint return one spouse can supply the ownership months, but each spouse must separately have the living months. Using the exclusion on a different house during the previous two years usually shuts it off.

  • Ownership months: 24 within the last 5 years.
  • Primary-residence months: 24 within the last 5 years.
  • No exclusion claimed on another sale in the past two years.
  • Extended-duty members of the military, Foreign Service or intelligence community can suspend the five-year count for up to 10 years.

For worksheets and exceptions, see IRS Publication 523, Selling Your Home.

Rentals and investment houses usually can't use the home sale exclusion, which leaves a taxable capital gain. If you held the property over a year the gain is long-term; at a year or less it is short-term and taxed at ordinary income rates.

For 2025 the long-term federal rate has three steps. It is 0% on taxable income up to $48,350 for single filers and $96,700 for joint filers, 15% from there to $533,400 single or $600,050 joint, and 20% beyond.

Landlords should know two more federal items. The slice of gain that comes from depreciation, called unrecaptured section 1250 gain, tops out at a 25% rate. Higher-income sellers may also face the net investment income tax (IRS Topic 559).

These federal rates stack on top of the Virginia rates above, because Virginia taxes the gain as income.

The formula is simple: amount realized minus adjusted basis. Your basis begins at the purchase price plus buying costs, rises for value-adding improvements, and falls for depreciation and casualty insurance payouts.

Hang on to receipts for roofs, additions and remodels, since each raises basis and cuts the taxable gain. If you sell your own home at a loss, there is no deduction.

  • Start from the contract price and settlement statement.
  • Raise your cost by documented capital improvements.
  • Lower it by depreciation if any part was rented out.
  • Compare what remains with the $250,000 or $500,000 cap.

Gifts and inheritances follow their own basis rules, spelled out in IRS Publication 551, Basis of Assets. Look there before you pick a number.

sections.h2: Order of work for a Virginia seller
sections.html:
If you are about to sell and want to know what tax to expect, work through it in this order.

  1. Label the property as your main home, a rental or an inheritance, because that label drives everything after it.
  2. If it is your main home, tally the months you owned and lived in it. Hitting 24 within the last 5 years generally settles the federal exclusion.
  3. Collect your purchase paperwork and the receipts for roofs, additions and remodels to build your basis.
  4. Confirm you haven't used the exclusion on another sale recently.
  5. Get the settlement statement from the closing agent, and expect a Form 1099-S later.
  6. Apply Virginia's brackets to any gain left over and set cash aside in case estimated payments are needed.

A tax professional can check each step. This list only shows what to ask.

Receiving a Form 1099-S, Proceeds From Real Estate Transactions, puts the sale on your return even when the entire gain is excludable. A partly taxable gain gets reported too, using Form 8949 and Schedule D where they apply.

When the buyer pays part of the price in a later year, the installment method applies unless you elect out. Spreading gain over time this way leaves the home sale exclusion intact.

IRS Publication 505 explains the estimated payments a large gain can trigger.

Two non-income-tax items shrink a Virginia seller's proceeds: the state grantor tax on the deed and any real estate tax still owed.

Code 58.1-802 sets the grantor tax at 50 cents on every $500 of consideration. The seller owes it unless the parties agree to another split. A clerk of court certifies it before the deed is recorded, and the state and locality each keep half.

Under Code 58.1-3340 the lien for real estate tax outranks all other liens. Sale proceeds go first to taxes and levies on the property, and your contract prorates your portion of the year's tax.

Billing calendars vary by locality. Virginia Beach collects on December 5 and June 5.

Inherited property isn't valued at what the decedent paid. Publication 551 explains how basis works for it, and Publication 544 handles holding periods for property from a decedent.

On a rental, claimed depreciation lowers basis and can create the section 1250 gain mentioned above. A tenant in the house raises lease questions too, and the Virginia eviction notice guide on this site covers them.

  • Inherited: confirm basis before you price the house.
  • Rental: add up depreciation across all your years of ownership.
  • Primary home: test the 24-month rules before an offer arrives.

sections.h2: Tax angle on a fast as-is sale
sections.html:
It can pay off when carrying costs, repairs or an approaching tax bill would cost you more than the discount. An early closing stops the monthly mortgage, insurance and property tax drain and gives you a set date for planning.

The buyer's identity doesn't alter your tax, because gain comes from price and basis. Speed changes your timing, your carrying payments and the repairs you skip.

Get a CPA or enrolled agent to run your figures before accepting anything. We buy houses as-is and can share a closing timeline, but tax advice isn't something we give.

faqs.q: Does Virginia have a capital gains tax?
faqs.a: There's no separate tax. Gain is treated as income at Virginia's ordinary rates, topping out at 5.75% above $17,000 under Code 58.1-320.

faqs.q: How much gain can I exclude when I sell my Virginia home?
faqs.a: As much as $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you've owned and lived in the house 24 months of the past 5 years. Virginia goes along with the federal rule.

faqs.q: Do I report the sale if the whole gain is excluded?
faqs.a: If a Form 1099-S came, yes, even with a fully excludable gain. You also report it when only part of the gain is excludable.

faqs.q: How long must I own a rental house for long-term capital gain treatment?
faqs.a: Over a year. Selling at one year or sooner produces a short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income.

faqs.q: Who pays the Virginia grantor tax?
faqs.a: Normally the seller, at 50 cents per $500 of consideration. A contract can shift part or all of it to the buyer.
